summary.text: A previously healthy 64-year-old man arrived at the emergency department on July 25, 2025, with a 1-week history of asthenia, febrile headache and altered mental status. His last travel outside France was to Portugal in 2016, and he had stayed in the Jura department in eastern France 3 weeks earlier. The table lists fever, headache, obnubilation and neck stiffness.

Initial lumbar puncture showed neutrophil-predominant meningitis (leukocytes 430 cells/L, 76% neutrophils) and elevated CSF protein of 1.19 g/L, without hypoglycorrhachia, and a multiplex neuromeningeal PCR panel was negative. A second lumbar puncture on hospitalization day 4 showed lymphocytic meningitis with 88% lymphocytes. Brain MRI was unremarkable, and blood and CSF were WNV positive by PCR and IgM. The table's protein and leukocyte rows carry each other's values.

Probabilistic treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone, amoxicillin, acyclovir and dexamethasone was started in the emergency department before admission to the intensive care unit. Neither patient had underlying immunodepression, C reactive protein was below 30 mg/L with negative procalcitonin, and the authors describe favorable outcomes for the patients.

ambiguities.issue: For the first lumbar puncture the text gives leukocytes 430 cells/L and CSF protein 1.19 g/L, while the table row labelled protein level gives 430 and the row labelled leukocyte count gives 1.19. For the second lumbar puncture the text gives leukocytes 48 cells/L, while the table row labelled protein level gives 48 and the leukocyte row gives 1.26. The magnitudes agree with the text but sit under each other's row labels, so this is read as a table labelling error rather than a value conflict.
ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not relabel or move the table cells between analytes and do not assign the table-only second-puncture magnitudes to a specific analyte; the text values stand as reported.

summary.text: A 25-year-old woman without any travel outside the Paris area during the past 4 years arrived at the ED on August 2, 2025, with fever, neck stiffness, binocular diplopia and vertigo without altered mental status, and had a 3-day history of influenza-like illness. She also had biochemical evidence of hepatic cytolysis. The table lists fever and headache.

Lumbar puncture showed lymphocytic meningitis (leukocytes 1,200 cells/L, 90% lymphocytes) with elevated CSF protein of 1.95 g/L, without hypoglycorrhachia, and a multiplex neuromeningeal PCR panel on the first CSF sample was negative. Brain MRI was unremarkable. A second lumbar puncture at 72 hours still showed lymphocytic meningitis with elevated protein and normal glucose. Blood and CSF were WNV positive by PCR and IgM. The table's protein and leukocyte rows carry each other's values.

Probabilistic treatment with cefotaxime, amoxicillin, gentamicin, acyclovir and dexamethasone was started in the ED before ICU admission. Clinical examination evolved to include a cerebellar syndrome with nystagmus, bilateral peripheral facial nerve paralysis, decreased reflexes in the lower limbs and acute urinary retention. She had no underlying immunodepression, C reactive protein below 30 mg/L and negative procalcitonin, and the authors describe favorable outcomes for the patients.

evidence.quote: Lumbar puncture showed lymphocytic meningitis (leukocytes, 1,200 cells/L with 90% lymphocytes) with elevated CSF protein (1.95 g/L)
Protein level, g/L (reference <0.40) | 430 | 1,200
Leukocyte count, cells/L (reference <0.05) | 1.19; 76% neutrophils | 1.95; 90% lymphocytes

ambiguities.issue: The text gives leukocytes 1,200 cells/L and CSF protein 1.95 g/L at the first lumbar puncture, while the table row labelled protein level gives 1,200 and the row labelled leukocyte count gives 1.95. The magnitudes agree with the text but sit under each other's row labels, so this is read as a table labelling error rather than a value conflict.
ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not relabel or move the table cells between analytes and do not assign the table-only second-puncture magnitudes to a specific analyte; the text values stand as reported.

A second lumbar puncture at 72 hours still showed lymphocytic meningitis with elevated CSF protein and normal glucose.

ambiguities.issue: For the second lumbar puncture the text gives no numbers, and the table rows give protein 260 and leukocyte count 1.4 with 75% lymphocytes. The table labels disagree with the text in the other comparable pairs, so the analyte labels of these cells are uncertain.
ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not treat 260 or 1.4 as confirmed protein or leukocyte values and do not link them to the text statement of elevated CSF protein.

article_limitations: No figures or supplements are listed in the source.

The Table 1 protein level and leukocyte count rows carry each other's magnitudes compared with the text for every pair that has a text value; this is recorded as a table labelling ambiguity: text values are kept as reported and table cells are kept as printed, review-only. Table values for the second lumbar puncture without a text counterpart (patient 1: 1.26; patient 2: 260 and 1.4) are review-only ambiguous.
The abstract sentence that one patient had not traveled outside Paris and the other had traveled to eastern France is not mapped to a case; patients are numbered by the case narrative and table.
The sentences on the WNV RNA and IgM detection methods and on exclusion of other flaviviruses (Usutu virus) do not say which patients they cover and are not assigned.
The discussion contrast between acute encephalitis with altered mental status and rhombencephalitis is not mapped to a patient.
The discussion mortality figure, the convalescent plasma trial, bird-migration hypotheses and the statement that the cases occurred days apart are not patient facts.
The Jura stay and the history durations use anchors that the source does not name explicitly; anchors left null or taken from the literal event wording.
